title: RESTCONF Protocol
summary: Describes an HTTP-based protocol that gives a programmatic interface for accessing data defined in YANG, using the datastore concepts from NETCONF. It lets tools manage network devices with ordinary web-style requests.

plainLanguage.summary: RESTCONF lets a program read and change network-device data with HTTP requests. The server's YANG modules describe the available data and help the client build requests.

subtitle: A YANG-driven HTTP interface for reading and changing network-device data.

tldr.problem: Web applications need a standard way to access a device's YANG-defined configuration, state, operations, and event notifications.
tldr.mechanism: RESTCONF maps HTTP methods to operations on YANG data, using NETCONF datastore concepts and XML or JSON message bodies over TLS.
tldr.outcome: Clients can derive resource paths and message structure from the server's YANG modules. RFC 8040 is updated by RFC 8527.

today: RFC 8040 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8527. The unit metadata does not list an obsoleting RFC.

sections.title: An HTTP Interface to YANG Data
sections.content:
RESTCONF is an HTTP-based protocol for accessing data defined with YANG and using NETCONF datastore concepts. It exposes configuration data, state data, data-model operations, and event notifications as resources.

Clients use HTTP methods to retrieve or edit data and encode bodies as XML or JSON. RESTCONF implements a subset of NETCONF functionality and is designed to be compatible with NETCONF datastores, not to replace NETCONF.
sections.plainLanguage: RESTCONF gives programs a web-style way to read and change network settings described by YANG. It uses some NETCONF concepts but has its own HTTP interface.

sections.title: A Data-Model-Driven Interface
sections.content:
A client that knows the YANG modules used by a server can derive resource paths and the structure of requests and responses. The server must implement the YANG library and identify all YANG modules it uses.

YANG statements tell the client whether data is configuration or state and how list data is ordered. Each edit is activated when it completes successfully.

If RESTCONF and NETCONF share a device, edits use the running datastore when NETCONF supports writable-running. Otherwise, edits use candidate and are committed immediately; an active NETCONF lock makes the RESTCONF edit fail.
sections.plainLanguage: The YANG modules describe the device's data, so a client can work out how to address it. The server applies each successful edit and must respect locks held through NETCONF.

sections.title: Secure Transport and User Identity
sections.content:
RESTCONF requires transport integrity and confidentiality. A server must support TLS and must not offer RESTCONF over unencrypted HTTP. It must support the https URI scheme and present an X.509v3 certificate.

The client must validate the server certificate or match it to a certificate obtained through a trusted method, and it must check the server identity. The server must authenticate access to protected resources. The identity derived from client authentication is the RESTCONF username and is subject to the NETCONF Access Control Model.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection must use TLS so others cannot read or change its data in transit. The client checks the server, and the server checks the client's identity and permissions.

sections.title: The API Root and Resource Paths
sections.content:
A client first discovers the RESTCONF API root by requesting /.well-known/host-meta and reading the restconf link. The root begins the path for later RESTCONF requests.

The mandatory data resource represents the device's configuration and state. The optional operations resource lists data-model RPC operations, and the mandatory yang-library-version leaf identifies the YANG library revision date.

Data-resource paths follow the YANG hierarchy. When a node comes from a different module, its module name prefixes the node name. List keys follow the list name in the URI, with reserved characters encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: The client discovers the API root, then builds a path through the YANG data tree. A path can name a module, a data node, and the keys that identify a list entry.

sections.title: HTTP Methods for Reading and Editing
sections.content:
RESTCONF uses HTTP methods to retrieve, create, replace, merge, and delete resources. GET reads data; POST creates a child or invokes an operation; PUT creates or replaces a resource; PATCH merges a plain-patch body; and DELETE removes a resource.

A successful creation returns 201 Created with a Location header. A replacement or deletion can return 204 No Content. A plain patch can create or update a child but cannot delete one, and it cannot create its target resource.

Query parameters can select configuration or state, limit returned depth, choose fields, filter event streams, control user-ordered list insertion, request event replay, or control default values. A repeated or unexpected parameter causes a bad-request error. Timestamps and entity-tags can help detect edit collisions.
sections.plainLanguage: Each HTTP method has a defined job, such as reading, creating, replacing, merging, or deleting data. Optional query parameters narrow a read or control how data is inserted.

sections.title: Notifications and Event Streams
sections.content:
A server may offer notification streams. A client lists available streams, reads a stream's location, and opens it with the text/event-stream media type. The connection then carries server-sent events.

A stream can identify its description, supported encoding, location, and whether it supports replay. If replay is available, the client can request a start time and optionally a stop time. An XPath filter can select events of interest.

The server advertises supported optional features as capability URIs. A later RESTCONF protocol version would use a different root resource and link relation.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can open an event stream and receive updates as the server sends them. It can ask for earlier events or filter the stream when the server supports those options.

sections.title: Access Control and Sensitive Configuration
sections.content:
Configuration data can include passwords, user names, service descriptions, and topology information. Sending it without confidentiality and integrity protection can expose it to eavesdropping or false data injection, so RESTCONF uses HTTPS with TLS.

The server applies the NETCONF access-control model to RESTCONF users and operations. The RFC recommends that servers avoid TLS 1.3 zero-round-trip data because it can create security problems for RESTCONF APIs. It also notes that HTTP authentication schemes differ in strength.
sections.plainLanguage: Device configuration can contain sensitive information, so RESTCONF protects the connection and restricts what each user can access. The RFC also advises servers not to use TLS zero-round-trip data for RESTCONF.
